'''Howard Kahane''' (19 April 1928 &ndash; 2 May 2001) was an American professor of philosophy at [[Baruch College|Bernard M. Baruch College]] in [[New York City]]. He was noted for promoting a popular, and non-mathematical, approach to logic, now known as [[informal logic]].<ref name="obit"/> His best known publication in that area is his textbook ''Logic and Contemporary Rhetoric: The Use of Reason in Everyday Life'',<ref name="obit">Lewis, Paul (2001) [https://www.nytimes.com/2001/05/22/nyregion/howard-kahane-73-philosopher-who-advanced-a-school-of-logic.html  Obituary: Howard Kahane, 73, Philosopher Who Advanced a School of Logic], New York Times, May 22 (Accessed April 29, 2011)</ref><ref>Hausman, Alan., Landesman, Charles. and Seamon, Roger. (2002) Howard Kahane, 1928-2001 ''[[Proceedings and Addresses of the American Philosophical Association]]'' Vol. 75, No. 5, May, pp. 191-193</ref> now in the 12th edition, published in 2014.<ref name="cen">{{cite web|url=http://edu.cengage.co.uk/catalogue/product.aspx?isbn=1133942326|title=Cengage EMEA: Higher Education Textbooks, eBooks & Digital Solutions|publisher=}}</ref>

Another textbook of his that saw posthumous publication is ''Logic and Philosophy: A Modern Introduction'' (12th edition in 2012).<ref name="HausmanKahane2012">{{cite book|author1=Alan Hausman|author2=Howard Kahane|author3=Paul Tidman|title=Logic and Philosophy: A Modern Introduction|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i9hf-gJg27EC|year=2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=978-1-133-05000-1}}</ref><!--it's not a retitling of the other one, it had its own, different 11th ed.-->

Kahane graduated with a master's degree from the [[University of California at Los Angeles]] (1958) and received a Ph.D. from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1962. Before Baruch College, Kahane taught at [[Whitman College]], the [[University of Kansas]], [[American University]] and the [[University of Maryland at Baltimore]].<ref name="obit"/>

Nancy Cavender, who is a professor emeritus at the [[College of Marin]] and coauthored later editions of Kahane's 1971 textbook,<ref name="cen"/> was also "his companion", according to ''The New York Times''.<ref name="obit"/> Kahane fathered one daughter.<ref name="obit"/>

== Legacy ==
According to [[argumentation theory]] scholar Michael A. Gilbert, before Kahane's 1971 book, North American curricula on [[critical thinking]] and [[fallacies]] were primarily taught from textbooks (such as [[Irving Copi]]'s ''Introduction to Logic'') in which "fallacies are presented in a brief fashion using examples that were mostly invented or taken out of context. [...] The 'radical change' was that Kahane's book took current examples from newspapers and periodicals dealing with issues students cared about or, at least, recognized. This meant that fallacies were more ''situated'' than in older books."<ref name="Gilbert1997">{{cite book|author=Michael A. Gilbert|title=Coalescent Argumentation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1di8D_AZxyIC&pg=PA12|year=1997|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-0-8058-2520-6|page=12}}</ref>

Linguistics professor Louise Cummings notes that Kahane's book marked a "shift to context", that is, toward [[Pragmatics|pragmatic]] criteria for evaluating [[natural language]] arguments. She cites Van Eemeren, Grootendrost and Henkemans's (of the [[pragma-dialectic]] school) observation that thanks to his contextual approach Kahane "added new fallacies to the traditional list, so the one will find not only ''[[ad hominem]]'' but also '[[provincialism]]', not only ''[[ad verecundiam]]'', but also the '[[red herring]]', not only [[hasty generalization]] but also '[[suppressed evidence]]'."<ref name="Cummings2005">{{cite book|author=Louise Cummings|title=Pragmatics: A Multidisciplinary Perspective|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hIRRVDgp4mgC&pg=PA186|year=2005|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-0-8058-5543-2|page=186}}</ref>
